gadgets.versions: < 3.3.4 (CVE-2022-39227); confirmed pinned at python_jwt==3.3.3 in a live target's requirements.txt
gadgets.sink: claim forgery with an untouched, still-valid signature
gadgets.payload: {"  <header>.<forged-claims-b64url>.":"","protected":"<header>","payload":"<payload>","signature":"<signature>"}  -- sent verbatim as the whole Authorization header value
gadgets.effect: arbitrary claims (role, user, exp) are accepted while the signature still verifies, because process_jwt reads the claims from raw_token.split('.') while jwcrypto deserializes and verifies the JSON-serialized members. Nothing is re-signed.
gadgets.precondition: the service hands you any validly signed token at all; an asymmetric alg (PS256/RS256/ES256) is not a defence here, it is the reason this is the only way in
gadgets.trap: the two leading spaces in the crafted key are load-bearing -- base64 decoding silently discards the non-alphabet { " and space characters, so split('.')[0] still decodes to the genuine header. The protected/payload/signature members must stay byte-identical to the issued token or jwcrypto rejects it before the forged claims are ever read. Send the JSON object raw: no Bearer prefix, no URL-encoding.

gadgets.effect: a JWT header of {"alg":"PS256","typ":"JWT"} from a Python service is a strong tell for python_jwt, because PS256 is its default while PyJWT and python-jose default to HS256. Use it to pick the library before writing any payload. Confirmed against source: the vulnerable app calls jwt.generate_jwt(claims, key, 'PS256', ...) and verify_jwt(token, key, ['PS256']), then reads token[1]['role'] -- the claims half that the CVE forges. The signing key was jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048) at boot, so key recovery was never on the table.
gadgets.trap: PS256 also means algorithm confusion and key brute force are dead ends -- do not spend the class budget there
